# MQF Advanced Programming project contract

## Objective

Complete both approaches for each of Q2, Q3, and Q4 in one reproducible repository.
Q2 compares Monte Carlo estimators and transaction-cost hedges on a GBM model calibrated from Chinese futures data.
Q3 compares classical and recurrent macroeconomic models using information available at each forecast date.
Q4 compares classical graph analytics and learned embeddings on a Chinese ownership or trade network.
The group owns the mathematical choices, verifies the results, and writes the report.
Confirm any methodological ambiguity with the group before making it part of the experiment.

## Environment and commands

Use Python 3.13 and `uv` with dependencies declared in `pyproject.toml` and pinned in `uv.lock`.
Run the current Q2 commands from the repository root.

```sh
export UV_CACHE_DIR="$PWD/.cache/uv"
uv sync --locked --python 3.13
uv run --locked python data/fetch.py --question q2 --offline
uv run --locked python code/approach1_q2.py --seed 42
uv run --locked python code/approach2_q2.py --seed 42
uv run --locked python code/compare.py
```

After installing dependencies, use `--offline` on the `uv` commands to test offline reproduction.
Add the Q3 and Q4 commands here and in the README as those approaches are integrated.

## Data and experiments

Commit offline fallback snapshots for every external source used.
Use `data/fetch.py` for retrieval and offline verification, and record source, query, retrieval date, schema, and SHA-256 in `data/metadata.json`.
Validate files before using them, and preserve the committed snapshots during experiment runs.
Q2 uses the fixed IF0, CU0, CSI 300, and SHIBOR snapshots for 2020 through 2025.
Use daily closes for Q2 calibration, document the continuous-contract roll convention, and keep simulation seeds for training, validation, and testing separate.
Verify the European prices against Black-Scholes in both engines and report the z-scores.
Save the Q2A estimator results, convergence plots, and profiles alongside its metrics.
For Q2B, report the hedged payoff and the CVaR, mean P&L, and P&L variance for each frequency and cost on held-out paths.
For Q3, use expanding-window validation, apply publication lags, and fit preprocessing within each training window.
For Q4, split link-prediction edges 80/10/10 before computing training graph features or embeddings.

Default to `--seed 42`, seed each stochastic step, and record residual nondeterminism.
Each approach exposes an argparse CLI and writes `results/approachN/<dataset>/metrics.json` using question-specific dataset names and the keys `params`, `metrics`, `fit_seconds`, and `history`.
Use Rich for terminal summaries and embed Plotly JavaScript in the saved HTML.
The comparison script writes `results/comparison.html` and ranks only comparable experiments.

## Session and Git rules

Use an approved OpenCode-compatible terminal agent for implementation.
Keep all writes and tool caches within the repository, and ignore local caches, environments, and credentials.
Obtain explicit approval in the coding session before destructive or irreversible operations.
Keep documented commands reproducible from a clean clone.
Commit completed milestones separately using conventional prefixes such as `data:`, `feat:`, `exp:`, and `report:`.
Export the complete coding session, redact secrets, and include the Markdown transcript in `SESSION.md`.
Tag the final reviewed commit `submission`.

generator=rng, dtype=dtype)\n    log_moves.mul_(vol * math.sqrt(dt)).add_((rate - vol**2 / 2) * dt)\n    relatives = log_moves.cumsum(dim=1).exp_().mul_(spot)\n    return torch.cat((torch.full((count, contract\n\n## Objective\n\nComplete both approaches for each of Q2, Q3, and Q4 in one reproducible repository.\nQ2 compares Monte Carlo estimators and transaction-cost hedges on a GBM model calibrated from Chinese futures data.\nQ3 compares classical and recurrent macroeconomic models using information available at each forecast date.\nQ4 compares classical graph analytics and learned embeddings on a Chinese ownership or trade network.\nThe group owns the mathematical choices, verifies the results, and writes the report.\nConfirm any methodological ambiguity with the group before making it part of the experiment.\n\n## Environment and commands\n\nUse Python 3.13 and `uv` with dependencies declared in `pyproject.toml` and pinned in `uv.lock`.\nRun the current Q2 commands from external source used.\nUse `data/fetch.py` for retrieval and offline verification, and record source, query, retrieval date, schema, and SHA-256 in `data/metadata.json`.\nValidate files before using them, and preserve the committed snapshots during experiment runs.\nQ2 uses the fixed IF0, CU0, CSI 300, and SHIBOR snapshots for 2020 through 2025.\nUse daily closes for Q2 calibration, document the continuous-contract roll convention, and keep simulation seeds for training, validation, and testing separate.\nVerify the European prices against Black-Scholes in both engines and report the z-scores.\nSave the Q2A estimator results, convergence plots, and profiles alongside its metrics.\nFor Q2B, report the hedged payoff and the CVaR, mean P&L, and P&L variance for each frequency and cost on held-out paths.\nFor Q3, use expanding-window validation, apply publication lags, and fit preprocessing within each training window.\nFor Q4, split link-prediction edges 80/10/10 before computing training graph features or embeddings.\n\nDefault to `--seed 42`, seed each stochastic step, and record residual nondeterminism.\nEach approach exposes an argparse CLI and writes `results/approachN/<dataset>/metrics.json` using question-specific dataset names and the keys `params`, `metrics`, `fit_seconds`, and `history`.\nUse Rich for terminal summaries and embed Plotly JavaScript in the saved HTML.\nThe comparison script writes `results/comparison.html` and ranks only comparable experiments.\n\n## Session and Git rules\n\nUse an approved OpenCode-compatible terminal agent for implementation.\nKeep all writes and tool caches within the repository, and ignore local caches, environments, and credentials.\nObtain explicit approval in the coding session before destructive or irreversible operations.\nKeep documented commands reproducible from a clean clone.\nCommit completed milestones separately using conventional prefixes such as `data:`, `feat:`, `exp:`, and `report:`.\nExport the complete coding session, redact secrets, and include the Markdown transcript in `SESSION.md`.\nTag the final reviewed commit `submission`.\n[project]\nname = "mqf"\nversion --locked python code/approach2_q2.py --seed 42 && uv run --locked python code/compare.py\n```\nThe runs use committed snapshots and write metrics and standalone HTML to `results/`.\nAfter installing # one stage of one question\npython3 run.py q2 --offline            # all stages of q2 without network\npython3 run.py all --offline           # every question, all execution stages\npython3 run.py all --stage index       # rebuild root results/comparison.html from saved outputs\npython3 run.py all --dry-run           # print verification and planned commands only\n```\n\nCLI: `python3 run.py {q1,q2,q4,all} [--stage {verify,approach1,approach2,compare,all,index}] [--seed 42] [--offline] [--dry-run]`.\nEvery selected execution stage verifies the committed snapshots first; `--verify-only` and `--stage index` need no uv.\n`--offline` requires each question's dependencies to be installed already; omitting it lets uv install dependencies but never refreshes vendor data.\n\nInside a python code/approach1_q2.py --seed 42\n```\n\n## Isolated environments and unchanged locks\n\nEach question keeps its original `pyproject.toml` and locked `uv.lock`; no dependency versions were merged or upgraded.\n`run.py` executes each script in a fresh subprocess with the working directory set to the question directory, so question-local packages (`common.py`, a `code/` package) cannot collide.\nThe launcher sets `UV_CACHE_DIR` to `.cache/uv`, `UV_PYTHON_INSTALL_DIR` to `.cache/uv/python`, and `UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT` to that question's own `.venv/`, so all caches and environments stay inside this repository.\n\n## What the launcher verifies\n\n- Q2 (`questions/q2/data/metadata.json`): for each dataset's `clean` entry, the launcher checks the SHA-256, the row count, the header order against the schema, strictly increasing unique ISO dates, and coverage of `first_date`/`last_date`.\n- Q1 and Q4 (`questions/qN/data/clean/metadata.json`): every declared artifact's SHA-256 and byte length; empty manifests, missing artifacts and paths escaping the question folder are rejected.\nVerification uses only standard-library hashing and CSV parsing, no uv and no third-party imports.\n\n## Cross-question index\n\nEach question's own `compare.py` writes `results/comparison.html` inside that question and ranks only experiments comparable within that question.\nThe root `results/comparison.html` produced by `run.py --stage index` (or by `python3 run.py all`) is only a standalone index that links to saved per-question comparisons and counts their saved `metrics.json` files.\nIt never ranks across questions because Q1, Q2 and Q4 metrics are not comparable with each other; linked pages are explicitly labeled as saved outputs.\n\n## Source provenance\n\nImported Executive summary\n\nThis project studies an annual directed trade network induced by China’s largest trade partners from 2014–2023. Approach 1 measures network structure, minimum spanning trees, Louvain communities, centrality, and temporal migration. Approach 2 implements node2vec with biased walks, skip-gram negative sampling, a learned bilinear link scorer, and three heuristic baselines. On the fixed 2023 held-out split, the best embedding configuration (`p=2`, `q=0.5`, dimension 64) reaches AUC 0.810 and average precision 0.847, compared with AUC 0.750 for preferential attachment, 0.745 for common neighbors, and 0.705 for Adamic–Adar.\n\n## 2. Data and network construction\n\nThe source is the keyless UN Comtrade preview API specified by the assignment. `data/fetch.py` first ranks partners by China’s latest anchor-year imports plus exports, selects 20 partners, and fixes the node set to China plus those partners for every year. It then retrieves reported exports for every induced reporter–partner pair. The committed clean snapshot contains 10 years, 21 country nodes, and 4,160 positive raw edge rows. Raw API responses are cached under the ignored `data/raw/` directory; `data/clean/metadata.json` records the retrieval timestamp, schema, source, and SHA-256 hashes.\n\nFor year `t`, the raw directed edge is\n\n\\[\nT_{ij,t}=\\text{primaryValue}_{ij,t},\n\\]\n\nmeasured in USD. Because all selected countries report some small positive bilateral flows, the unfiltered induced graph is nearly complete and cannot support equal negative sampling. The analysis graph therefore keeps the six largest export edges per reporter per year. This rule is fixed before evaluation, is applied identically across years, and leaves the unfiltered clean snapshot available for audit. Self-loops are excluded by construction and checked in every run.\n\nThe assignment’s stock-industry labels are not defined for country nodes. We therefore use geographical region as a clearly labelled proxy only for community comparison; the primary Q4-B task is held-out trade-edge recovery rather than industry prediction.\n\n## 3. Reproducibility\n\nThe environment is Python 3.13 with dependencies pinned in `pyproject.toml` and `uv.lock`. The global default seed is 42. The canonical commands are:\n\n```bash\nuv sync\npython data/fetch.py --seed 42\npython code/approach1_network_analytics.py --seed 42 --top-k 6\npython code/approach2_node_embeddings.py --seed 42 --top-k 6\npython code/compare.py\n```\n\nEach approach uses the required CLI, writes `results/approachN/trade/metrics.json` with `params`, `metrics`, `fit_seconds`, and `history`, and writes self-contained Plotly HTML figures.\n\n## 4. Approach 1: network analytics\n\nThe directed graph is converted to an undirected weighted graph by summing reciprocal export weights. The metric used for the Kruskal minimum spanning tree is\n\n\\[\nd_{ij}=\\frac{1}{\\log(1+w_{ij})},\n\\]\n\nso larger trade relationships have shorter distances. We report node count, edge count, density, mean degree, a log–log degree-frequency slope, assortativity, connected components, isolated nodes, and self-loops. Louvain maximizes the weighted modularity\n\n\\[\nQ=\\frac{1}{2m}\\sum_{ij}\\left(A_{ij}-\\frac{k_i k_j}{2m}\\right)\\mathbf{1}(c_i=c_j).\n\\]\n\nPageRank uses damping 0.85. Betweenness uses shortest paths, and weighted degree sums trade values. Resolution sensitivity is evaluated at 0.5, 1.0, and 1.5. Consecutive-year migration is reported as an aligned contingency matrix and ARI.\n\n### 4.1 Graph statistics\n\n| Year | Nodes | Undirected edges | Density | Communities | Modularity | MST diameter | Assortativity |\n|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n| 2014 | 21 | 96 | 0.300 | 5 | 0.261 | 6 | -0.342 |\n| 2015 | 21 | 97 | 0.300 | 4 | 0.241 | 6 | -0.344 |\n| 2016 | 21 | 94 | 0.300 | 4 | 0.243 | 5 | -0.315 |\n| 2017 | 21 | 96 | 0.300 | 4 | 0.241 | 6 | -0.325 |\n| 2018 | 21 | 94 | 0.300 | 4 | 0.236 | 7 | -0.344 |\n| 2019 | 21 | 94 | 0.300 | 4 | 0.238 | 7 | -0.298 |\n| 2020 | 21 | 97 | 0.300 | 4 | 0.214 | 6 | -0.276 |\n| 2021 | 21 | 95 | 0.300 | 4 | 0.217 | 6 | -0.283 |\n| 2022 | 21 | 91 | 0.286 | 4 | 0.225 | disconnected | -0.292 |\n| 2023 | 21 | 91 | 0.286 | 4 | 0.230 | 6 | -0.277 |\n\nThere are no self-loops. One isolated node is reported in 2022; it is not silently removed. The 2023 top PageRank nodes are the United States, China, Mexico, Germany, and Japan. The 2023 resolution sweep produces 1, 4, and 6 communities at resolutions 0.5, 1.0, and 1.5 respectively.\n\n![Network evolution](results/approach1/trade/network_evolution.html)\n\n## 5. Approach 2: node2vec and link prediction\n\nFor a walk with previous node `t`, current node `v`, and candidate next node `x`, the node2vec transition bias is\n\n\\[\n\\alpha_{pq}(t,x)=\n\\begin{cases}\n1/p & x=t,\\\\\n1 & (t,x)\\in E,\\\\\n1/q & \\text{otherwise},\n\\end{cases}\n\\]\n\nmultiplied by the observed edge weight before normalization. Walk contexts use a window of two. The skip-gram objective uses positive context pairs and five uniformly sampled negative contexts:\n\n\\[\n\\log\\sigma(z_v^\\top c_u)+\\sum_{r=1}^{5}\\log\\sigma(-z_v^\\top c_{n_r}).\n\\]\n\nThe final-year graph is split into 80/10/10 positive edges and an equal number of negative non-edges: 72/9/10 in train/validation/test. The learned link score is\n\n\\[\ns(u,v)=\\sigma(z_u^\\top Wz_v),\n\\]\n\nwhere `W` is fitted only on the training split. Baselines are common neighbors, Adamic–Adar, and preferential attachment. We report AUC, average precision, and k-means agreement with Louvain and the region proxy using ARI/NMI.\n\n### 5.1 Dimension comparison at `p=1,q=1`\n\n| Dimension | Learned AUC | Learned AP | Common-neighbor AUC | Adamic–Adar AUC | Preferential-attachment AUC |\n|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n| 8 | 0.680 | 0.648 | 0.745 | 0.705 | 0.750 |\n| 16 | 0.710 | 0.755 | 0.745 | 0.705 | 0.750 |\n| 32 | 0.720 | 0.754 | 0.745 | 0.705 | 0.750 |\n| 64 | 0.740 | 0.798 | 0.745 | 0.705 | 0.750 |\n\n### 5.2 `p,q` sensitivity\n\n| Configuration | Best dimension | Best AUC |\n|---|---:|---:|\n| p=0.5, q=0.5 | 8 | 0.790 |\n| p=0.5, q=1 | 64 | 0.620 |\n| p=0.5, q=2 | 8 | 0.660 |\n| p=1, q=0.5 | 8 | 0.700 |\n| p=1, q=1 | 64 | 0.740 |\n| p=1, q=2 | 8 | 0.680 |\n| p=2, q=0.5 | 64 | **0.810** |\n| p=2, q=1 | 8 | 0.740 |\n| p=2, q=2 | 8 | 0.700 |\n\nAt the best configuration, average precision is 0.847. Embedding clusters have ARI 0.069 and NMI 0.249 against Louvain, and ARI 0.016 and NMI 0.293 against the region proxy. Thus the embedding is more useful for edge recovery than for reproducing the classical community partition.\n\n![Link prediction](results/approach2/trade/link_prediction.html)\n\n## 6. Limitations and checks\n\nThe preview API provides reported values and does not guarantee a complete reconciled world trade matrix. The fixed 21-node induced network is intentionally manageable and is not a full global network. The top-k rule improves link-prediction identifiability but changes the interpretation from all reported flows to major relationships. Country regions are not industry labels, so region agreement is explicitly a proxy rather than evidence of industry alignment. The test set is small; AUC and AP are reported together and should not be overinterpreted. Future work would use a larger country universe, multiple HS levels, repeated temporal test windows, and bootstrap uncertainty intervals.\n\n## 7. Division of work\n\nThe terminal workflow implemented the data retrieval, checksum metadata, graph construction, estimators, benchmarks, figures, and reproducibility scaffolding. The group is responsible for reviewing mathematical definitions, checking the generated results, approving the top-k and proxy-label assumptions, and making the final claims.\n'}]

Executive summary\n     4\t\n     5\tThis project estimates China CSI 300 option implied-volatility surfaces using public CFFEX historical contract data. Approach 1 performs quote filtering, Black–Scholes inversion, put–call parity diagnostics, constrained SVI calibration, repricing, and no-arbitrage checks. Approach 2 compares differentiable PyTorch SVI calibration with SciPy and trains a price-space neural surface with butterfly/calendar penalties. The liquid quote pipeline retains 225 quotes, successfully inverts 224, fits 12 SVI groups, obtains zero butterfly-grid violations, and has 1.67% median liquid-strike repricing error. Under a 30% quote-drop experiment, SVI obtains 0.067% median relative price error on held-out quotes and the neural surface obtains 0.204%.\n     6\t\n     7\t## 2. Data and provenance\n     8\t\n     9\tThe data pipeline uses the assignment-approved `akshare` interfaces: `option_cffex_hs300_spot_sina` and `option_cffex_hs300_daily_sina` for contract strikes and daily OHLCV, `stock_zh_index_daily(symbol="sh000300")` for the CSI 300 index, and `macro_china_shibor_all` for the historical 3M SHIBOR rate. The snapshot contains nine expiry months, 1,134 raw call/put quote rows, 177 observed dates, and a date range from 2023-03-20 to 2026-01-13. A shared October 2023 block contains four expiries on five dates, enabling calendar diagnostics.\n    10\t\n    11\tFor every selected contract, the fetcher keeps the first five trading dates within a 31-calendar-day window and 13 evenly spaced strikes. It also keeps a common 2023-10-23 through 2023-10-27 block for four overlapping expiries when the contract traded on those dates. Raw responses are cached in ignored `data/raw/`; clean snapshots and SHA-256 hashes are committed in `data/clean/metadata.json`.\n    12\t\n    13\tThe formal liquid-quote rule is volume at least 40 and forward moneyness `0.9 <= K/F <= 1.1`. Market definitions\n    16\t\n    17\tFor quote date `t`, spot `S`, continuously compounded rate `r`, time to expiry `T`, and zero dividend yield, the forward is\n    18\t\n    19\t\\[\n    20\tF=S e^{rT}, \\qquad D=e^{-rT}.\n    21\t\\]\n    22\t\n    23\tFor volatility `sigma`,\n    24\t\n    25\t\\[\n    26\td_1=\\frac{\\log(F/K)+\\frac12\\sigma^2T}{\\sigma\\sqrt{T}},\n    27\t\\qquad d_2=d_1-\\sigma\\sqrt{T}.\n    28\t\\]\n    29\t\n    30\tThe Black–Scholes forward prices are\n    31\t\n    32\t\\[\n    33\tC=D(FN(d_1)-KN(d_2)),\n    34\t\\qquad P=D(KN(-d_2)-FN(-d_1)).\n    35\t\\]\n    36\t\n    37\tImplied volatility is obtained separately for every call and put using bracketed Brent root finding on `[10^-4, 5]`. generator=rng, dtype=dtype)\n    log_moves.mul_(vol * math.sqrt(dt)).add_((rate - vol**2 / 2) * dt)\n    relatives = log_moves.cumsum(dim=1).exp_().mul_(spot)\n    return torch.cat((torch.full((count, 1), spot, dtype=dtype), relatives), dim=1)\n\n\ndef payoff_tensors(paths, strike, barrier):\n    terminal = paths[:, -1]\n    european = (terminal - strike).clamp_min(0)\n    return {\n """Prepare the decision grid and the short-call payoff in units of S0."""\n    steps = paths.shape[1] - 1\n    indices = list(range(0, steps, rebalance_days))\n    prices = paths[:, indices + [steps]] weight at the empirical cutoff.\n    tail_count = losses.numel() * (1 - CVAR_ALPHA)\n    worst = losses.topk(math.ceil(tail_count), sorted=True).values\n    return (worst.sum() - (worst.numel() - best_loss = math.inf\n    best_epoch = 0\n    best_weights = None\n    history = []\n\n    for epoch in range(1, EPOCHS + 1):\n        for indices in torch.randperm(len(payoff), Greeks: delta and vega by (i) pathwise estimator (e.g. $\\delta = e^{-rT}\\,\\mathbb{E}[\\mathbf{1}_{S_T > K} S_T / S_0]$ for vanilla), (ii) central finite differences with bump $h \\in \\{10^{-1}, 10^{-2}, 10^{-3}\\} S_0$; report bias–variance tradeoff.\n3. Convergence: RMSE vs. $N$ on log–log, all estimators; verify $O(N^{-1/2})$ slope.\n4. Performance: vectorized `numpy` engine vs. naive loop implementation; `timeit` before/after; profiling of the hot loop (line_profiler or equivalent) included in the report.\n\n### 4.4 Option B — Deep hedging (PyTorch)\n\n1. Simulator as §4.2 with proportional transaction cost $\\kappa$.\n2. Hedging strategy: $\\Delta_t^{\\theta} = f_{\\theta}(S_t/S_{t_0}, t)$, MLP ($\\le 3$ hidden layers); terminal P&L\n   $V_T = \\sum_{t} e^{r(T-t)}\\Delta_{t}(S_{t+\\Delta t} - S_t) - \\kappa\\sum_t |\\Delta_t - \\Delta_{t-1}| S_t - \\text{option payoff}$.\n3. Objective: minimize CVaR$_\\alpha$ of $-V_T$ (empirical $\\alpha = 0.95$ quantile-based loss), train on simulated paths (≥ $2^{17}$), validate on independent seeds.\n4. Benchmarks: Black–Scholes delta hedging at rebalancing frequencies $\\{1, 5, 21\\}$ days and cost levels $\\kappa \\in \\{0, 10, 50\\}$ bp; report CVaR$_\\alpha$, variance, expected P&L tables; sensitivity of the learned strategy to $\\kappa$.\n\n### 4.5 Benchmarks (indicative)\n\nNaive-vs-control-variate variance reduction factor ≥ 5 on the Asian payoff; pathwise/finite-difference delta agreement within reported standard errors.\n\n---\n\n## 5. Question 3 — China macro panel: regimes, nowcasting, indicator clustering\n\nCourse mapping: Sessions 2–3 (pandas, datetime, clustering, SQL), Session 3 KMeans. Skills: panel construction with publication lags, factor models, classification, hierarchical clustering, honest temporal validation.\n\n### 5.1 Data (public, verified)\n\n| Item | Source |\n|---|---|\n| 170 `macro_china_*` interfaces: GDP, CPI, PPI, PMI (NBS & Caixin), M0/M1/M2, 社融 (TSF), LPR, Shibor, retail sales, industrial output, industrial profits, exports/imports YoY, trade balance, consumer confidence, electricity output, … | `akshare` `macro_china` family |\n| Offline fallback | committed snapshot `data/clean/macro_panel.csv` |\n\nBuild a monthly panel $x_{i,t}$, $i = 1,\\dots,d \\ge 20$, ≥ 10 years, with per-series publication lag $L_i$ documented in `metadata.json`. Information set discipline:\n$\\mathcal{F}_t = \\{x_{i,s} : s + L_i \\le t\\}$; any use of $x_{i,s}$ with $s + L_i > t$ is leakage and a grading fault.\n\n### 5.2 Common requirements\n\n- Panel hygiene: missing-value report; outlier rule (e.g. MAD) stated; transformations (logs, YoY, Sa) documented per series; standardized panel $\\tilde x_{i,t} = (x_{i,t} - \\mu_i)/s_i$ with statistics from training windows only.\n- Regime label: contraction indicator $d_t = \\mathbf{1}\\{\\text{PMI}_{t} < 50 \\text{ and } \\text{PMI}_{t-1} < 50\\}$ (state and justify the labeling; sensitivity to the 49.5 threshold reported).\n- Validation: expanding-window walk-forward; metrics: Brier score, AUC, accuracy; naive prior-frequency baseline reported alongside.\n\n### 5.3 Option A — Classical\n\n1. Factor model: PCA on $\\tilde x_t$; choose rank $r$ by cross-validated nowcast error; $\\tilde x_t = \\Lambda f_t + \\varepsilon_t$.\n2. Nowcasting bridge: $\\hat y_{t} = \\beta_0 + \\beta^\\top f_t$ for quarterly GDP growth (or monthly industrial output), estimated on $\\mathcal{F}_{t}$ only; nowcast revision path within the quarter reported.\n3. Regime model: probit $\\mathbb{P}(d_{t+1} = 1) = \\Phi(\\beta^\\top z_t)$, $z_t$ = factors + yield/spread controls; coefficient table with standard errors.\n4. Indicator clustering: distance $d_{ij} = \\sqrt{2(1 - \\rho_{ij})}$ on rolling 3-year correlations, Ward linkage; dendrogram; cluster stability via adjusted Rand index across adjacent windows; relate clusters to lead/lag cross-correlations with GDP.\n\n### 5.4 Option B — Sequence learning (PyTorch)\n\n1. Sequence model (LSTM/GRU, ≤ 2 layers, dropout reported): input = window of $\\tilde x_{t-h:t}$, output $\\mathbb{P}(d_{t+1}=1)$; class imbalance handled explicitly (weighting or threshold selection on validation).\n2. Latent macro states: hidden-state embeddings $h_t$; $k$-means on $\\{h_t\\}$; compare clusters with the Option-A correlation clusters (ARI/NMI) and with the regime labels.\n3. Comparison: Brier/AUC of (i) probit baseline, (ii) LSTM, (iii) LSTM without lag discipline (intentional leakage demo, reported as the leakage premium — this ablation is mandatory).\n4. Training discipline: early stopping on walk-forward validation; seeds × 3, mean ± std reported.\n\n### 5.5 Benchmarks (indicative)\n\nRegime AUC ≥ 0.75 walk-forward (classical baseline); nowcast error vs. a random-walk-with-drift benchmark; leakage ablation quantified.\n\n---\n\n## 6. Question 4 — China financial and trade networks\n\nCourse mapping: Session 3 (KMeans, SQL, imbalance). Skills: graph construction, community detection, centrality, node embeddings, link prediction.\n\n### 6.1 Data (public, verified)\n\n| Network | Source |\n|---|---|\n| A-share shareholding: top-10 (circulating) shareholders per stock per quarter | `akshare` `stock_gdfx` interfaces (46 endpoints, Eastmoney) |\n| Fund holdings: fund–stock quarterly portfolios | `ak.fund_portfolio_hold_em(symbol=..., date=...)` |\n| China trade partners: annual bilateral flows (HS, partner-level) | UN Comtrade public API, keyless: `comtradeapi.un.org/public/v1/preview/C/A/HS?reporterCode=156&period=...` |\n| Industry classification (ground truth) | `ak.stock_board_industry_*` / SW industry |\n\nPrimary network (choose one, or both as A/B contrast): ownership network or trade network. Snapshot: ≥ 8 quarters (ownership) or ≥ 10 years (trade).\n\n### 6.2 Common requirements\n\n- Construction rules stated as mathematics: e.g. correlation network $w_{ij} = \\sqrt{2(1-\\rho_{ij})}$ (price networks), bipartite holdings $B \\in \\{0,1\\}^{|F| \\times |S|}$ with weighted projection $W = B^\\top B$ (fund–stock), directed weighted trade graph $T_{ij}$ (value of exports $i \\to j$).\n- Graph statistics table per period: $|V|$, $|E|$, density, degree distribution (log–log fit), assortativity, connected components.\n- Verification duty: assert no self-loops, symmetric treatment where required, isolated nodes reported.\n\n### 6.3 Option A — Network analytics (networkx)\n\n1. Minimum spanning tree (Kruskal) of the metric distance network; evolution of tree diameter across periods.\n2. Community detection: Louvain, modularity\n   $Q = \\frac{1}{2m}\\sum_{ij}\\Big[A_{ij} - \\frac{k_i k_j}{2m}\\Big]\\,\\delta(c_i, c_j)$;\n   compare communities with industry classification via ARI/NMI; resolution-sensitivity sweep.\n3. Centrality: degree, betweenness, PageRank (iterative solution of $p = \\alpha P^\\top p + (1-\\alpha)\\mathbf{1}/n$, $\\alpha = 0.85$); ranked tables; interpretation (systemic firms / dominant trade partners).\n4. Temporal analysis: community migration matrix between consecutive periods; identify structurally central nodes and structural breaks.\n\n### 6.4 Option B — Node embeddings and link prediction (PyTorch)\n\n1. node2vec (own implementation of the biased-walk skip-gram): objective $\\max_\\theta \\sum_v \\sum_{u \\in \\mathcal{N}(v)} \\log p_\\theta(u \\mid z_v)$; walk parameters $(p, q)$ swept.\n2. Link prediction: score $s(u,v) = \\sigma(z_u^\\top W z_v)$; edges split 80/10/10 with equal negative sampling; metrics AUC, average precision; baselines: common-neighbors, Adamic–Adar, preferential attachment.\n3. Task framing (choose per network): recover held-out holdings edges; predict industry membership from $z_v$ (linear probe); predict future trade-link formation $\\Delta T_{ij} > 0$.\n4. Clustering the embedding space ($k$-means on $z_v$) vs. Louvain communities vs. industry labels (ARI/NMI matrix); embedding dimension swept $\\{8, 16, 32, 64\\}$.\n\n### 6.5 Benchmarks (indicative)\n\nLink-prediction AUC ≥ 0.75 vs. ≥ 0.65 for the best heuristic baseline; ARI(embedding clusters, industry) reported against ARI(Louvain, industry).\n\n---\n\n## Appendix — Data source registry (verified 2026-10)\n\n| Source | Access | Status |\n|---|---|---|\n| akshare (MIT, 23k★, active) | `pip install akshare`, aliyun mirror | public |\n| SSE option chains (`option_current_day_sse`, daily stats) | akshare → sse.com.cn | public |\n| CFFEX index option contract lists & daily OHLCV | akshare → Sina Finance | public |\n| `macro_china_*` (170 series incl. Asian, barrier and digital prices above do not imply that those payoffs were separately hedged.\n+A two-hidden-layer width-16 MLP maps $(S_t/S_0,t)$ to a bounded position.\n+The experiment uses the assignment's terminal accounting $V_T=\\sum_t e^{r(T-t)}\\Delta_t(S_{t+\\Delta t}-S_t)-\\kappa\\sum_t|\\Delta_t-\\Delta_{t-1}|S_t-(S_T-K)^+$.\n+Entry trade cost is charged with $\\Delta_{-1}=0$; no option premium is added and no terminal stock liquidation cost is charged under this stated convention.\n+Negative expected P&L therefore includes the sold claim's value and must not be interpreted as a premium-inclusive trading loss.\n+The empirical training loss is the mean of the worst 5% sample losses, a quantile-tail CVaR95 approximation.\n+Each cost/frequency case trains on at least $2^{17}=131,072$ paths, validates on 8,192 independent paths and tests on 32,768 held-out paths.\n+Adam uses learning rate 0.003 and batches of 4,096, with at most 100 epochs.\n+Checkpoint selection uses only S0-normalized validation CVaR, patience ten and minimum improvement $10^{-5}$.\n+The table reports actual trained epochs, best validation epoch and termination reason; reaching the epoch cap is not proof of convergence.\n+The Black-Scholes hedge and learned hedge share the same held-out paths for each case.\n+\n+\"\"\"\n+    rows=[]\n+    for c,r in runs.items():\n+        for key,v in r['approach2']['metrics']['hedging'].items():\n+            h=r['approach2']['history']['hedging'][key]\n+            rows.append([c.upper(),v['rebalance_days'],v['cost_bps'],v['deep']['cvar95'],v['bs']['cvar95'],v['deep']['mean_pnl'],v['bs']['mean_pnl'],v['deep']['pnl_variance'],v['bs']['pnl_variance'],f\"{h['epochs_run']} / {h['best_epoch']}\",h['stopping_reason']])\n+    text += table([\"Contract\", \"Days\", \"Cost bp\", \"Learned CVaR\", \"BS CVaR\", \"Learned mean\", \"BS mean\", \"Learned variance\", \"BS variance\", \"Epochs / best\", \"Stop\"],rows)\n+    wins=sum(v['deep']['cvar95']<v['bs']['cvar95'] for r in runs.values() for v in r['approach2']['metrics']['hedging'].values())\n+    text += f\"\\nThe learned strategy has lower held-out CVaR in {wins} of 18 cases; no claim of universal outperformance is supported.\\nTransaction costs penalize frequent position changes, so the interaction with rebalancing frequency matters more than a single headline score.\\nOnly seed 42 is the primary experiment; robustness across training seeds and confidence intervals for CVaR differences remain limitations, not assignment-required results that have been silently assumed.\\nSeeded CPU training uses two threads and can retain last-bit differences across platforms.\\nFigures and validation histories: [NumPy IF0](results/approach1/if0/figures.html), [NumPy CU0](results/approach1/cu0/figures.html), [hedging IF0](results/approach2/if0/figures.html), [hedging CU0](results/approach2/cu0/figures.html) and [comparison](results/comparison.html).\\n\"\n+    return text\n+\n+\n+def q4_report():\n+    a=read('questions/q4/results/approach1/trade/metrics.json')['metrics']\n+    b=read('questions/q4/results/approach2/trade/metrics.json')['metrics']\n+    f=read('questions/q4/results/approach2/trade_future/metrics.json')['metrics']\n+    text=r\"\"\"# Q4. Chinese trade network analytics and prediction\n+\n+## Data, graph definition and verification\n+\n+The committed UN Comtrade preview snapshot covers ten annual periods, 2014 through 2023, for 21 nodes selected from China's 2023 major trading partners.\n+Queries use annual merchandise exports, HS TOTAL, partner-level USD values, and the fixed reporter/partner set documented in the [manifest](data/clean/metadata.json).\n+Snapshot verification checks actual hashes, schema, year coverage, unique reporter/partner/year keys and positive finite flow values.\n+This public preview sample is neither a complete global trade network nor an industry-level dataset.\n+The 2023-selected country universe is retrospective, even when experiments use earlier graph years.\n+Country-region labels are geographical proxies, with some original unclassified partner codes retained as Other; they are not industry ground truth.\n+This is an explicit deviation from the assignment's industry-label comparison and requires group or instructor acceptance for a country-level trade network.\n+\n+For each year, $T_{ij}$ is reported exports from $i$ to $j$ and only each reporter's six largest positive exports within the sampled universe are retained.\n+The weighted directed graph has one edge for each retained $T_{ij}>0$, excludes self-loops and retains isolated nodes.\n+For undirected analysis, $W_{ij}=T_{ij}1_{retained(i,j)}+T_{ji}1_{retained(j,i)}$; verification checks the exact edge union and reciprocal-weight sum.\n+Distances are $d_{ij}=1/\\log(1+W_{ij})$ on existing edges, so larger trade means shorter distance.\n+This monotone edge dissimilarity need not satisfy the triangle inequality; the Kruskal tree is a minimum spanning tree of the observed connected graph, not a proven Euclidean metric network.\n+Directed and undirected densities use their respective edge counts and denominators $n(n-1)$ and $n(n-1)/2$.\n+The descriptive log-log slope regresses log positive degree-frequency counts on log positive degree support without dropping the first bin; 21 nodes do not support a power-law inference.\n+All annual graphs have zero self-loops, and isolates and connected components are reported explicitly.\n+\n+## Classical annual statistics and communities\n+\n+\"\"\"\n+    text += table([\"Year\", \"V\", \"Directed E\", \"Undirected E\", \"Directed density\", \"Undirected density\", \"Degree slope\", \"Assortativity\", \"Components\", \"Isolates\", \"MST diameter\", \"Louvain Q\"],[[y,v['nodes'],v['directed_edges'],v['undirected_edges'],v['directed_density'],v['undirected_density'],v['degree_loglog_slope'],v['assortativity'],v['connected_components'],v['isolated_nodes'],v['mst']['diameter'],v['communities']['modularity']] for y,v in a['per_year'].items()])\n+    text += r\"\"\"\n+Louvain optimizes weighted modularity $Q=(2m)^{-1}\\sum_{ij}[W_{ij}-\\gamma k_i k_j/(2m)]1_{c_i=c_j}$, where $k_i$ is weighted degree and $m=\\frac12\\sum_{ij}W_{ij}$.\n+The primary resolution is one, with seeded sweeps at 0.5, 1 and 1.5.\n+PageRank uses directed trade weights, damping 0.85 and uniform teleportation: $p=0.85P^\\top p+0.15\\mathbf1/n$.\n+Weighted directed betweenness uses the same decreasing-trade distance convention; undirected weighted degree is the sum of reciprocal retained flows.\n+The United States and China are the top two PageRank nodes in 2014 and 2023, reflecting centrality within this selected network rather than a claim about the full world economy.\n+\n+### 2023 resolution sensitivity\n+\n+\"\"\"\n+    text += table([\"Resolution\", \"Communities\", \"Modularity\", \"ARI vs region proxy\", \"NMI vs region proxy\"],[[k,v['community_count'],v['modularity'],v['ari_vs_region_proxy'],v['nmi_vs_region_proxy']] for k,v in a['per_year']['2023']['resolution_sweep'].items()])\n+    text += \"\\n### Ranked 2023 centralities\\n\\n\"\n+    text += table([\"Metric\", \"Rank\", \"Country / original code label\", \"Value\"],[[metric,row['rank'],row['name'],row['value']] for metric,rows in a['per_year']['2023']['centrality_rankings'].items() for row in rows])\n+    text += \"\\nFull country-named rankings and degree distributions for every year are retained in [classical metrics](results/approach1/trade/metrics.json).\\nConsecutive community matrices retain their original row and column labels; Hungarian one-to-one matching removes arbitrary label permutations while preserving real splits and merges.\\nChanged share counts nodes that remain unmatched after this matching, and ARI is independently label-invariant.\\n\\n\"\n+    text += table([\"Transition\", \"Changed share\", \"ARI\", \"Split previous labels\", \"Merged current labels\", \"Raw contingency matrix\"],[[k,v['changed_share'],v['ari'],v['split_previous_labels'],v['merged_current_labels'],v['contingency']] for k,v in a['community_migration'].items()])\n+    text += \"\\nThe largest observed migration is 2014 to 2015; changes also occur in 2021 to 2022 and 2022 to 2023.\\nThese are structural changes in detected sample communities, not identified causal breaks in trade policy.\\nIn 2022 to 2023 the raw matrix preserves one previous community splitting into two and a corresponding merge, instead of collapsing both into a matched label.\\n\\n\"\n+    text += r\"\"\"## Embeddings and corrected static edge benchmark\n+\n+The weighted node2vec walk moves from previous node $t$ through current node $v$ to neighbor $x$ with weight $W_{vx}\\alpha_{pq}(t,x)$, where $\\alpha=1/p$ for returning to $t$, one for neighbors of $t$, and $1/q$ otherwise.\n+Skip-gram maximizes $\\log\\sigma(z_v^\\top c_u)+\\sum_{j=1}^5\\log\\sigma(-z_v^\\top c_{n_j})$ using its own PyTorch implementation and degree-to-the-3/4 negative sampling.\n+The bilinear link classifier is $s(u,v)=\\sigma(z_u^\\top Bz_v)$; binary cross entropy trains $B$ using training labels only.\n+The static 2023 graph has 91 undirected positive edges, split into 72 training, nine validation and ten test positives, with equal disjoint negative sampling in each split.\n+The split occurs before walks, embeddings, Louvain or baseline graph features are computed.\n+All validation and test positive edges are absent from the 72-edge training graph; exact pairs and graph fingerprints are saved.\n+We sweep $p,q\\in\\{0.5,1,2\\}$ and dimensions $\\{8,16,32,64\\}$, selecting by validation AUC, then validation AP and deterministic parameter tie-breaks.\n+The final test labels are scored once for the selected model and are never used to select a dimension or walk parameters.\n+Common-neighbor, Adamic-Adar and preferential-attachment scores are all computed on that same training graph.\n+\n+\"\"\"\n+    text += f\"Selected static parameters: p={b['selection']['selected_p']}, q={b['selection']['selected_q']}, dimension={b['selection']['selected_dimension']}.\\nThe historical full-graph/test-selected AUC is superseded by the corrected scores below.\\n\\n\"\n+    text += table([\"Static test method\", \"AUC\", \"Average precision\"],[[k,v['auc'],v['average_precision']] for k,v in {'learned':b['learned'],**b['baselines']}.items()])\n+    text += \"\\n### Complete clustering agreement matrix (unique pairs)\\n\\n\"\n+    text += table([\"Label pair\", \"ARI\", \"NMI\"],[[k,v['ari'],v['nmi']] for k,v in b['model_agreement']['pairs'].items()])\n+    text += r\"\"\"\n+## Future major-trade-link formation\n+\n+The additional temporal task predicts $Y_{ij,t+1}=1$ when an undirected relation absent from the year-$t$ top-six graph appears in year $t+1$.\n+This is formation of a major retained trade relation, not the first occurrence of any positive raw bilateral trade and not a continuous dollar-flow forecast.\n+Train transitions are 2014 to 2015 through 2020 to 2021; validation is 2021 to 2022; the final test is 2022 to 2023.\n+The static 80/10/10 split remains a separate benchmark; the temporal task uses chronological splits to preserve forecasting order.\n+Each transition embeds only its forecast-year graph, with equal sampled negatives among absent relations that stay absent in the target year.\n+Embedding orientations are aligned by orthogonal Procrustes against the first training-year embedding using node identities, without future labels.\n+A shared bilinear matrix is trained on training transitions only; walk parameters and dimension are selected on validation only.\n+The fixed node universe is selected retrospectively from 2023, so the result is conditional on these countries rather than a fully prospective population forecast.\n+\n+\"\"\"\n+    text += table([\"Transition\", \"Train positive\", \"Train negative\"],[[f\"{v['feature_year']} to {v['target_year']}\",v['positive_count'],v['negative_count']] for v in f['training_transitions']])\n+    text += f\"\\nValidation has {len(f['validation_sample']['positive'])} positive and {len(f['validation_sample']['negative'])} negative examples.\\nThe final test has only {len(f['test_sample']['positive'])} positive and {len(f['test_sample']['negative'])} sampled negative examples, from {f['test_sample']['population_negative']} available nonformations.\\nThis tiny holdout gives a very coarse and unstable AUC, so it cannot establish forecasting skill.\\nSelected temporal parameters are p={f['selection']['p']}, q={f['selection']['q']}, dimension={f['selection']['dimension']}, with validation AUC {fmt(f['selection']['validation_auc'])}.\\n\\n\"\n+    text += table([\"Future test method\", \"AUC\", \"Average precision\"],[[k,v['auc'],v['average_precision']] for k,v in {'learned':f['learned'],**f['baselines']}.items()])\n+    text += \"\\nBoth learned tasks miss the indicative AUC target of 0.75.\\nThe static Adamic-Adar baseline exceeds the indicative 0.65 heuristic target, but the temporal benchmark does not.\\nPoor final test performance is retained honestly and is not used to retune the experiment.\\nAverage precision is measured on balanced case-control samples, so it does not estimate precision at the population's actual formation prevalence.\\nThe region-proxy comparison does not fulfill a literal industry-ground-truth requirement.\\nSeed 42 governs splits, walks, negative sampling, optimization and clustering;
